early_blight.name: Early Blight
early_blight.description: Early Blight is caused by the soil-borne fungus Alternaria solani. It is one of the most common and economically significant tomato diseases in Sri Lanka and tropical regions. Despite its name, it can occur at any growth stage.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings (bull's-eye pattern) on older lower leaves
Spots enlarge and merge causing leaf yellowing and defoliation
Defoliation starts from the base of the plant and moves upwards
Dark sunken lesions can also appear on fruits and stems
Severely affected leaves drop prematurely reducing yield
favorable_conditions: High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness
Overcrowded plants with poor air circulation

chemical.dosage: 32g per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 14 days — do not harvest fruit within 14 days of the last spray
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Fungicides section, Crop 14 (Potato and Tomato), Early Blight. Alternate with a systemic fungicide. Start spraying after first symptoms. Maximum 3 applications per season.

chemical.dosage: 40g per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 14 days — do not harvest fruit within 14 days of the last spray
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Fungicides section, Crop 14 (Potato and Tomato), Early Blight. Corrected from an earlier version of this knowledge base which had the wrong dosage and litre-basis — verified directly against the source document.

chemical.dosage: 32g per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 14 days — do not harvest fruit within 14 days of the last spray
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Fungicides section, Crop 14 (Potato and Tomato), Early Blight. This is a WG (water dispersible granule/powder) product, measured in grams, not millilitres — corrected from an earlier version of this knowledge base which incorrectly listed it in ml.
Broad-spectrum protectant. Apply to upper and lower leaf surfaces. Reapply after rain.
Highly effective systemic fungicide. Research shows up to 65% disease reduction over control.

biological.notes: Research shows Bacillus velezensis promotes plant growth and enhances defense enzyme activities against Alternaria solani. Environmentally friendly alternative to chemical fungicides.

application_tips: Apply fungicides at the INITIAL stage of disease development — do not wait until severe infection
Spray both upper AND lower leaf surfaces thoroughly
Apply to the point of runoff for complete coverage
Reapply after heavy rainfall
Alternate between different fungicide groups to prevent resistance development
Apply in early morning or late afternoon to avoid heat stress on plants

application_volume.ml_per_mature_plant: 150-200ml of mixed spray solution for one fully-grown plant, sprayed to the point of run-off (leaves visibly wet, droplets just starting to drip)
application_volume.note: Younger or smaller plants need less; large, bushy plants may need more. This is a coverage-based estimate, not a fixed dose — spray until the leaves are wet, not by a strict volume target.
application_volume.minimum_practical_batch: The DOA dosages above are given per 16-litre knapsack sprayer, the standard local sprayer size — mixing a full 16L batch for just 1-2 plants is wasteful and hard to measure down accurately. Prepare a minimum of 1 litre instead (1/16 of the listed dose, e.g. 2g Mancozeb 80% WP in 1L water), enough for roughly 5-6 mature plants at 150-200ml each. For a single plant, prepare this 1L batch and discard the unused portion rather than trying to measure a fraction of a gram.
application_volume.source: Per-plant coverage volume (150-200ml) is general agricultural extension guidance, not yet confirmed from a DOA Sri Lanka-specific source. The underlying per-16L product dosages themselves ARE DOA-sourced (DOA_SL_PEST_2019) — see the chemical treatment entries above, which also include the pre-harvest interval (PHI) for each product.

practices: Use disease-resistant or tolerant tomato varieties (e.g., DOA released varieties: Thilina, KWR, Ravi, Maheshi)
Practice crop rotation — do not plant tomatoes or other Solanaceae crops in the same field for at least 2-3 years
Remove and destroy infected plant debris immediately after harvest — do not compost
Remove infected leaves from the base of the plant as soon as symptoms appear
Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip or furrow irrigation to keep foliage dry
Water plants in the morning so foliage dries before nightfall
Maintain proper plant spacing (80cm x 50cm as recommended by DOA Sri Lanka) for good air circulation
Stake or trellis plants to keep foliage off the ground
Remove weeds regularly — weeds can harbor the pathogen and increase disease pressure
Apply well-decomposed organic matter (10 t/ha) to improve soil health
Maintain balanced fertilization — potassium and calcium strengthen plant cell walls reducing susceptibility
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes lush growth susceptible to disease
Maintain soil pH between 5.5-7.5 as recommended by DOA Sri Lanka
Ensure good soil drainage to reduce root stress
Treat seeds with Captan or Thiram (2g per 125g of seeds) before sowing — DOA Sri Lanka recommendation
Use virgin lands or heat-sterilized soil for nursery beds
Start with healthy certified seedlings
Harden seedlings before transplanting
Inspect plants regularly (at least twice a week) especially during humid conditions
Begin preventive fungicide spray program before symptoms appear if conditions are favorable
Monitor weather — apply protective fungicide spray before expected rainy or humid periods

late_blight.name: Late Blight
late_blight.severity: Very Severe — Can destroy entire crop rapidly
late_blight.description: Late Blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans, a highly destructive pathogen historically responsible for the Irish Potato Famine. In Sri Lanka and tropical regions, it can spread extremely rapidly under cool, wet conditions and destroy an entire tomato crop within days if not managed promptly.
symptoms: Irregular dark green to brown water-soaked spots on leaves, often surrounded by a pale yellow-green halo
White-grayish mold (sporulation) visible on the underside of leaves under high humidity
Spots rapidly enlarge and turn dark brown to black causing complete leaf death
Dark water-soaked lesions on stems — stem lesions can girdle and kill entire branches
Dark, firm, brown lesions on fruits — affected fruits quickly rot
Disease spreads extremely rapidly — entire field can be destroyed in 7-10 days under favorable conditions
Distinctive foul smell from rotting affected tissue
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (10°C - 20°C) with high relative humidity (>90%)
Poor air circulation in dense plantings
Night temperatures below 20°C with warm days

chemical.dosage: 32g per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 14 days — do not harvest fruit within 14 days of the last spray
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Fungicides section, Crop 14 (Potato and Tomato), Late Blight. Must be applied PREVENTIVELY before disease onset — less effective once disease is established. Maximum 3 applications per season.

chemical.dosage: 50g per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 14 days — do not harvest fruit within 14 days of the last spray
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Fungicides section, Crop 14 (Potato and Tomato), Late Blight. Contains a systemic component for better control than contact fungicides alone. Corrected from an earlier version of this knowledge base which had the wrong dosage and litre-basis.

chemical.dosage: 32g per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 14 days — do not harvest fruit within 14 days of the last spray
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Fungicides section, Crop 14 (Potato and Tomato), Late Blight. This is a WG (water dispersible granule/powder) product, measured in grams, not millilitres — corrected from an earlier version of this knowledge base.

chemical.dosage: 16ml per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 14 days — do not harvest fruit within 14 days of the last spray
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Fungicides section, Crop 14 (Potato and Tomato), Late Blight.

chemical.interval: 3-5 days after application another fungicide needed
chemical.notes: Good curative activity but short residual — must be tank-mixed with a protectant fungicide.
Research shows excellent control (≥75%) of late blight. Apply preventively.

biological.notes: Research (2024) shows RS65 treatment reduced late blight severity from 31.26% to 16.54%. Promising sustainable alternative. Not yet widely commercially available.
Copper provides some protective control especially in organic production. Apply preventively. Not effective once disease is established.

application_tips: CRITICAL: Apply fungicides PREVENTIVELY — late blight is extremely difficult to control after detection
Increase spray frequency to every 5-7 days during cool wet weather
Apply systemic fungicides (Metalaxyl mixtures) for better penetration into plant tissue
Always tank-mix mobile/systemic fungicides with a protectant fungicide
Alternate fungicide groups to prevent resistance — P. infestans develops resistance rapidly
Remove and destroy severely infected plant material immediately
Do NOT compost infected material — destroy by burning
Spray equipment can spread spores — clean thoroughly between fields

application_volume.ml_per_mature_plant: 150-200ml of mixed spray solution for one fully-grown plant, sprayed to the point of run-off (leaves visibly wet, droplets just starting to drip)
application_volume.note: Younger or smaller plants need less; large, bushy plants may need more. This is a coverage-based estimate, not a fixed dose — spray until the leaves are wet, not by a strict volume target.
application_volume.minimum_practical_batch: The DOA dosages above are given per 16-litre knapsack sprayer, the standard local sprayer size — mixing a full 16L batch for just 1-2 plants is wasteful and hard to measure down accurately. Prepare a minimum of 1 litre instead (1/16 of the listed dose, e.g. 2g Mancozeb 80% WP in 1L water), enough for roughly 5-6 mature plants at 150-200ml each. For a single plant, prepare this 1L batch and discard the unused portion rather than trying to measure a fraction of a gram.
application_volume.source: Per-plant coverage volume (150-200ml) is general agricultural extension guidance, not yet confirmed from a DOA Sri Lanka-specific source. The underlying per-16L product dosages themselves ARE DOA-sourced (DOA_SL_PEST_2019) — see the chemical treatment entries above, which also include the pre-harvest interval (PHI) for each product.

practices: Use resistant tomato varieties when available — ask DOA Sri Lanka (HORDI, Gannoruwa) for currently recommended resistant varieties
Avoid planting in low-lying areas with poor air movement
Maintain proper plant spacing (80cm x 50cm) for good air circulation
Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip or furrow irrigation
Water plants in the morning only — allow foliage to dry during the day
Remove and destroy all infected plant debris immediately after harvest
Practice crop rotation — do not plant tomatoes or potatoes (same pathogen) in same field for 2-3 years
Do not bring infected transplants into a clean field
Remove volunteer tomato and potato plants which can harbor the pathogen
Monitor weather forecasts — cool temperatures (10-20°C) with rain or high humidity signal high risk
Begin preventive fungicide applications before symptoms appear when weather favors disease
Inspect lower leaves and undersides of leaves for early symptoms
Act immediately at first sign of infection — do not delay treatment
Inform neighboring farmers if late blight is detected — spores spread by wind and can infect nearby fields
Remove all crop debris and destroy after harvest
Avoid working in infected fields when plants are wet — spores spread on clothing and equipment
Work in infected fields last — do not move from infected to healthy fields
Clean and disinfect equipment between fields
Do not store infected fruits or plant material near healthy plants
Ensure good soil drainage — waterlogged conditions favor P. infestans
Apply balanced fertilization — avoid excess nitrogen
Use well-decomposed organic matter to improve soil structure and drainage

leaf_miner.name: Leaf Miner
leaf_miner.scientific_name: Tuta absoluta (Sri Lanka DOA's official designation for tomato leaf miner damage, under Polytunnel Pests); visually similar serpentine mining can also be caused by Liriomyza spp. leaf-mining flies on other crops
leaf_miner.type: Insect Pest (Leaf-mining moth larvae, also bores fruit at later stages)
leaf_miner.severity: Mild to Moderate on leaves alone — mainly reduces photosynthesis and cosmetic quality; this pest can also bore into fruit, which is more economically damaging, so it should not be dismissed as purely cosmetic
leaf_miner.description: Leaf miner damage on Sri Lankan tomato is officially attributed by the DOA (Pesticide Recommendations 2019, Polytunnel Pests) to Tuta absoluta, whose larvae tunnel through leaf tissue creating winding pale/white trails, and can progress to boring fruit. Globally, visually similar serpentine leaf mines are also caused by Liriomyza leaf-mining flies on various crops.
symptoms: Winding, serpentine white to pale tunnels (mines) visible on the leaf surface, following an irregular trail
Small white speckled puncture marks from adult feeding/egg-laying, often clustered near the trail
Tunnels widen progressively as the larva grows inside
Heavily mined leaves may yellow, dry out, and drop prematurely
Multiple overlapping mines can occur on a single leaf under heavy infestation
Unlike blight, damage does not spread as dark lesions — it stays confined to visible tunnel trails
favorable_conditions: Warm weather favors rapid leaf miner fly reproduction
Dense plantings with heavy foliage give more egg-laying sites
Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides that kill the natural parasitoid wasps which normally keep leaf miner populations in check
Nearby host weeds or previous infested crops carrying over adult flies

chemical.dosage: 6g per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.interval: minimum 7 days between applications, only if damage is seen
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 10 days — do not harvest fruit within 10 days of the last spray
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Insecticides section, Crop 06 (Tomato — Polytunnel Pests), Leaf Miner/Fruit Borer (Tuta absoluta). Apply only for larvae control.

chemical.dosage: 10ml per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.interval: minimum 7 days between applications, only if damage is seen
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 14 days — do not harvest fruit within 14 days of the last spray
chemical.type: Contact + translaminar (moves short distance into leaf tissue)
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Insecticides section, Crop 06 (Tomato — Polytunnel Pests), Leaf Miner/Fruit Borer (Tuta absoluta). Apply only for larvae control.

chemical.dosage: 6ml per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.interval: minimum 7 days between applications, only if damage is seen
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 14 days — do not harvest fruit within 14 days of the last spray
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Insecticides section, Crop 06 (Tomato — Polytunnel Pests), Leaf Miner/Fruit Borer (Tuta absoluta). Apply only for larvae control.

chemical.dosage: 4g per 16 litres of water (standard knapsack sprayer)
chemical.interval: minimum 7 days between applications, only if damage is seen
chemical.pre_harvest_interval: 14 days — do not harvest fruit within 14 days of the last spray
chemical.notes: Official DOA Sri Lanka Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Insecticides section, Crop 06 (Tomato — Polytunnel Pests), Leaf Miner/Fruit Borer (Tuta absoluta). Apply only for larvae control.

biological.agent: Parasitoid wasps (e.g. Diglyphus isaea, Opius spp.)
biological.notes: Naturally occurring parasitoid wasps lay eggs inside leaf miner larvae and are often the single biggest control factor in the field. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticide sprays that kill these wasps, as doing so can make leaf miner infestations worse, not better. DOA Sri Lanka research has specifically evaluated Diglyphus isaea release rates for Liriomyza huidobrensis management in Sri Lanka's Up Country Wet Zone — consult DOA HORDI for current release-rate guidance.

application_tips: IMPORTANT (DOA official notes): Apply insecticides ONLY for larvae control, not as a blanket preventive spray
Apply at a minimum of 7 days between sprays, only if damage is actually seen
This pest shows high resistance development — do NOT repeat the same insecticide in consecutive applications; rotate between different products and combine with IPM practices
Remove and destroy heavily mined leaves by hand — this directly removes larvae before they mature
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides where possible — they kill the natural parasitoid wasps that usually keep leaf miner populations low
Use yellow sticky traps near plants to monitor and reduce adult fly/moth numbers
Always observe the pre-harvest interval (PHI) for the specific product used before harvesting fruit

application_volume.ml_per_mature_plant: 150-200ml of mixed spray solution for one fully-grown plant, sprayed to the point of run-off (leaves visibly wet, droplets just starting to drip)
application_volume.note: Same general coverage principle as fungicide sprays — younger/smaller plants need less. Since leaf miner larvae are protected inside the leaf tissue, thorough coverage matters more for controlling adults/eggs than for reaching the larvae directly.
application_volume.minimum_practical_batch: The DOA dosages above are already given per 16-litre knapsack sprayer, which is the standard local sprayer size. If treating only 1-2 plants, mixing a full 16L batch is wasteful and impractical to measure down; prepare a minimum of 1 litre instead (1/16 of the listed dose), enough for roughly 5-6 mature plants at 150-200ml each.
application_volume.source: Per-plant coverage volume is general agricultural extension guidance, not yet confirmed from a DOA Sri Lanka-specific source. The underlying per-16L product dosages themselves ARE DOA-sourced (DOA_SL_PEST_2019) — see the chemical treatment entries above.

practices: Inspect young leaves regularly — remove and destroy leaves with active mines before larvae mature into adults
Practice crop rotation and avoid planting near previously infested Solanaceae crops
Remove and destroy host weeds near the field that can harbor leaf miner flies
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization — lush, soft growth is more attractive to egg-laying females
Minimize broad-spectrum insecticide use to protect naturally occurring parasitoid wasps
Where possible, choose selective products (e.g. spinosad, neem-based) over broad-spectrum options to preserve natural enemies
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor adult fly activity and time interventions
Inspect plants at least twice a week, especially younger leaves, for early mine trails

notes.text: If both Early Blight and Late Blight are detected on the same plant, you do NOT need two separate fungicide products. Per DOA Sri Lanka's official Pesticide Recommendations (2019), Mancozeb 80% WP, the Mancozeb 64% + Metalaxyl 8% WP combination, and Metiram 55% + Pyraclostrobin 5% WG are each officially listed for BOTH Early Blight and Late Blight — one spray of any of these products, at the dosage listed for that product, treats both diseases at once. Use whichever dosage/interval is listed for the disease present, and if the two overlap in interval, follow the shorter (more frequent) interval to be safe for both.

notes.topic: Leaf Miner + either fungal blight (insect + fungus)
notes.text: Leaf Miner is an insect/moth pest, not a fungus — a fungicide (used for Early/Late Blight) cannot control it, and an insecticide cannot control a fungal disease. If Leaf Miner is detected together with Early Blight and/or Late Blight, you need BOTH a fungicide (for the blight) AND a separate insecticide (for the leaf miner) — there is no single product that treats both categories. To save time, the fungicide and insecticide sprays can often be tank-mixed and applied together in one spray trip on the same day, but only if the specific products are chemically compatible — always check the product labels for tank-mix compatibility, or test a small batch first, before combining. This knowledge base does not have a DOA-verified list of specific compatible tank-mix pairs, so when in doubt, apply them as separate sprays or consult DOA Sri Lanka (HORDI, Gannoruwa) for compatibility advice.

notes.topic: All three detected together (Early Blight + Late Blight + Leaf Miner)
notes.text: Use one fungicide product effective against both blights (see the Early+Late Blight guidance above) PLUS one insecticide for Leaf Miner (see the Leaf Miner treatment options) — this is two products/sprays total, not three, since one fungicide already covers both fungal diseases. These two sprays can potentially be tank-mixed into one application if compatible; otherwise apply as two separate sprays, prioritizing whichever problem looks more severe first if time/resources are limited.
notes.source: Derived from the two notes above (DOA_SL_PEST_2019 for the fungicide overlap; general IPM guidance for the tank-mix caveat)

general_ipm.title: Integrated Pest Management for Tomato Diseases in Sri Lanka
principles: Use certified disease-free seeds and healthy transplants
Select DOA Sri Lanka released varieties suited to your agroclimatic zone
Follow recommended spacing and fertilization guidelines
Practice regular field monitoring — early detection is key
Use fungicides as a last resort and follow DOA pesticide recommendations
Always follow pesticide label instructions for dosage and safety
Wear protective equipment when applying fungicides
Observe pre-harvest intervals strictly before consuming or selling produce
